result: CIB2 and CIB3 have functionally redundant roles in mouse vestibular hair cells. Single knockouts of either Cib2 or Cib3 show normal vestibular function and FM 1-43 dye uptake, but double knockout mice (Cib2KO/KO;Cib3KO/KO) exhibit severe vestibular deficits including impaired VOR, circling behavior, head bobbing, and complete loss of FM 1-43 uptake in vestibular hair cells without hair cell degeneration.
evaluation: Reviewers note that 'many of the basic results from the mouse have already been reported by other groups in Liang et al. (2021) and Wang et al. (2023),' indicating that the vestibular findings are confirmatory rather than novel. While the data are described as 'necessary and convincing' in some parts, the lack of novelty and overlap with prior publications reduces confidence in treating these as new contributions.

result: In zebrafish, Cib2 and Cib3 are both required for normal MET function in lateral-line hair cells. Loss of cib2 alone significantly reduces acoustic startle responses and FM 1-43 labeling in lateral-line hair cells, while cib3 mutants show normal responses. Double mutants (cib2;cib3) show complete absence of startle responses, FM 1-43 labeling, and mechanosensitive calcium responses in lateral-line hair cells.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly state that 'their demonstration of the importance of CIB2 and CIB3 in zebrafish hair cell function is novel' and note that 'the results largely coincide with what is seen in the mouse.' The zebrafish studies are regarded as 'necessary and convincing,' indicating reviewer acceptance of these findings as a significant contribution.

result: In zebrafish, Cib2 is specifically required for MET function in hair cell subtypes that express Tmc2a. In the lateral line, Cib2 is essential for anterior flow-responsive cells (which express Tmc2b and Tmc2a), while Cib3 can compensate in posterior flow-responsive cells (which express primarily Tmc2b). In the crista, Cib2 is required in both short cells (Tmc2a-expressing) and tall cells (Tmc2b/Tmc1-expressing), while Cib3 is required only in tall cells.
evaluation: Reviewers note that 'cib2 is uniquely localized in and important for specific hair cell types in the neuromast and crista,' highlighting this as a novel and interesting finding. The specificity of Cib2 requirement for different hair cell subtypes is treated as a significant discovery that adds to understanding of the system.

result: AlphaFold 2 modeling predicts that CIB proteins simultaneously interact with at least two cytoplasmic domains of TMC1 and TMC2 (the N-terminus and IL1 domain), with CIB proteins 'clamped' between these domains. These predictions are validated by NMR spectroscopy showing simultaneous binding of TMC1-NT and TMC1-IL1 to CIB2 and CIB3, and are consistent with prior structural data including the crystal structure of TMC1-IL1 with CIB3.
evaluation: Reviewers state that 'structural studies (AlphaFold 2 modeling, NMR structure determination, and molecular dynamics simulations) brings us closer to the structure of the mammalian TMCs' and that this work 'offers significant new findings.' The structural work is praised for supporting 'the assignment of the TMC pore to alpha helices 4-7' and for providing a framework to reconcile contradictory prior results.

result: Molecular dynamics simulations predict that CIB proteins structurally stabilize TMC cytoplasmic domains and that TMC1 and TMC2 form cation channels. Simulations show that TMC N-termini are highly mobile without CIB proteins but become stable when CIB2 or CIB3 are present. Ion permeation simulations demonstrate K+ conductance with values reaching up to ~138 pS for TMC1, consistent with expected MET channel conductance, and suggest that CIB2 binding may enhance TMC1 conductance.
evaluation: While reviewers acknowledge the computational work as part of the manuscript, one reviewer notes that 'the grounding of the experimental and computational parts is different, and the firmness of conclusions, respectively, is not matched.' This suggests uncertainty about the strength of conclusions drawn from simulations compared to experimental data. The reviewer's comment that 'different components pull the emphasis in several directions with little cross-talk' indicates concerns about integration of computational and experimental findings.

result: Cib2KO/KO;Cib3KO/KO double knockout mice are profoundly deaf with no ABR responses to click or tone burst stimuli, show no FM 1-43 dye uptake in auditory hair cells, and exhibit progressive degeneration of auditory hair cells, confirming that CIB2 is indispensable for hearing and MET function in auditory hair cells.
evaluation: Reviewers explicitly note that 'many of the basic results from the mouse have already been reported by other groups in Liang et al. (2021) and Wang et al. (2023)' and describe parts of the paper as 'confirmatory studies' rather than novel findings. The auditory phenotype data are treated as replicating prior work rather than providing new insights.

result: Expression analysis shows that all four Cib family members are expressed in mouse inner ear tissues, but only Cib2 and Cib3 are expressed in immature and mature utricular hair cells (both type I and type II). Tmc1 is highly expressed in immature utricular hair cells while Tmc2 expression is low but increases during development, remaining below Tmc1 levels in mature hair cells.
evaluation: These expression data provide context for the functional studies and are not specifically critiqued by reviewers. The data support the rationale for focusing on CIB2 and CIB3 in vestibular hair cells and are treated as supporting evidence for the main findings.

result: The combined in vivo studies in mouse and zebrafish, along with structural modeling showing conserved architecture across species (including similarity to nematode TMC-1/CALM-1 complex), demonstrate that TMC1/2 and CIB2/3 proteins form functionally conserved complexes that are integral to hair-cell MET across vertebrate species and sensory organs.
evaluation: Reviewers acknowledge that the authors 'try to combine the three parts with the overarching theme of demonstrating that CIB2/3 play a functionally conserved role across species and hair cell types.' While one reviewer suggests the manuscript could be split, the conservation theme is treated as valid. The statement that the work provides 'a comprehensive look at the CIB family in hair cells' supports this integrative conclusion.
